transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. I’m just tired all the time and don’t have the energy to do much of anything anymore, even the stuff I used to enjoy. My wife finally insisted I come in because it feels like I'm just going through the motions every day.
How long have you been feeling this way, and would you say this is a relatively new change or something that has been going on for years?

This isn't a new change; it's actually been going on for a few years now. It really started settling in not long after I began phasing into retirement, about three years ago. Since then, this low, worn-out feeling has pretty much stuck with me.
During these past three years, have there been any periods of a few months where you felt completely back to your normal self, or has this low mood been present almost every day?

No, there haven't been any breaks where I felt back to my normal self. It's just been like a continuous low, gray cloud hanging over me almost every single day since I transitioned into retirement. It has pretty much stuck with me the whole time.
During these past three years, have you experienced any significant changes in your appetite, sleep patterns, or feelings of self-worth?

Yes, all three have been a mess. My appetite is highly inconsistent—I'll often forget to eat until late afternoon, or just mindlessly snack on junk food in front of the TV. When I try to sleep, my mind spins with worries about wasting my retirement before I wake up around 4 AM unable to drift back off, mostly because I've lost my sense of purpose and constantly worry if I'm even useful anymore.

Have there been any periods during these three years where your symptoms were so severe that you felt completely unable to function or experienced a total loss of interest in almost all activities for two weeks or longer?

No, I haven't had any sudden, severe spikes or specific two-week periods where I was completely unable to function. It's just been a steady, continuous "low, gray cloud" at a pretty consistent level since my retirement. It's more that I've gradually let things slide and felt constantly worn out rather than having distinct, severe episodes.
Have you ever experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt significantly worse than your usual 'low' state, perhaps feeling completely hopeless or unable to get out of bed at all?

No, I haven't really experienced a distinct two-week period where things got suddenly much worse or completely hopeless. It has just been a constant, steady low and gray feeling ever since I retired. I just feel like I'm dragging along at this same level every day.

inference_history.note: The patient reports persistent fatigue, anhedonia, and a general sense of being 'numb' or 'going through the motions.' These symptoms are highly suggestive of mood disorders. F32.9 (Major depressive disorder, single episode) and F33.9 (Major depressive disorder, recurrent) are primary considerations. F34.1 (Dysthymia) is considered due to the chronic nature of the 'tired all the time' complaint. F43.21 (Adjustment disorder with depressed mood) is included as a differential depending on whether these symptoms are linked to a specific recent stressor, which has not yet been established.

The patient reports a chronic (3-year) duration of low mood and anhedonia, which points more strongly toward a persistent mood disturbance rather than a single episode or an adjustment disorder. F34.1 is now prioritized over F32.9/F33.9 due to the duration and the insidious onset associated with a life transition (retirement). F43.21 is less likely given the duration and lack of clear acute stressor/recovery timeline.
